summary: Comments from UCLA-CCN to the author of RFC 226 on her proposed host names. They support having standard names but object to the list, suggesting NIC site codes as a better base, questioning the length limit, and noting the list covers fewer hosts than were then on the network.

eli5.summary: A reply to a naming plan: good idea, but the list is not complete or well chosen. Here are better choices.

subtitle: Technical critique of proposed ARPANET host naming scheme

tldr.problem: RFC 226 proposed a set of host mnemonics (short names) for Telnet users, but the proposal has significant flaws in its logic and completeness.
tldr.mechanism: The UCLA-CCN group responds with detailed critiques of the naming list, proposing instead that NIC site codes be used as the basis, and pointing out that the proposed list is incomplete and does not cover all known hosts.
tldr.outcome: This RFC exemplifies the early collaborative process of the ARPANET, where technical disagreements were hashed out in writing. The discussion influenced how naming standards evolved.

today: RFC 239 is an informational document and has not been obsoleted. It documents a constructive disagreement in the ARPANET standards process and reflects the collaborative engineering culture of the early network.

sections.title: Critique of RFC 226
sections.content: UCLA-CCN agrees that standardizing host names is a good idea, but objects to the specific list proposed in RFC 226. The response identifies the list as reflecting historical choices made by TENEX Telnet programmers rather than a principled approach to naming.
sections.eli5: The reply says: yes to standard names, but no to this particular list.

sections.title: Better Source for Names
sections.content:
UCLA-CCN proposes using NIC site codes as the foundation for host mnemonics instead. The NIC codes were chosen carefully and would become familiar to users as the Network Information Center grew. This would be more principled than relying on one programmer's choices.

The critique also questions why mnemonics should be limited to six characters, and points out that the RFC 226 list covers only 20 hosts when the most recent ARPANET roster lists 40. Using an incomplete list as a standard is problematic.
sections.eli5: The NIC codes are better because they were thought out, people already know them, and they cover all the computers.

sections.title: Specific Disagreements
sections.content: UCLA-CCN proposes concrete changes: UCLA91 instead of UCLA36 for their Sigma 7, and SRINIC instead of SRIARC for host 2 at Stanford Research Institute (because everyone calls it the NIC, not ARC). The reply emphasizes that standards deserve careful thought rather than perpetuating historical accidents.
sections.eli5: For example, people call one computer the NIC, so its short name should reflect that rather than preserving an old choice.

references.text: Karp, P., "Proposed host-host protocol", RFC 226, September 1971.
Bhushan, A., "Status of the ARPANET", RFC 208, August 1971.
